step: Multiply by the total usage of 500 billion litres:  [box expects: 100]
why: The box has no unit label and the sentence never says the answer should be given 'in billions'. A student who correctly computes 0.2 x 500 = 100 has no cue that they should type '100' rather than the full number (100,000,000,000) or '100 billion' — this is the exact scale-ambiguity trap.
fix: Label the box 'billion litres', or reword to 'Multiply 500 by your decimal (staying in billions of litres):'

step: Check: agriculture in the same way, in billions of litres =  [box expects: 350]
why: This is a dangling clause with no verb — 'agriculture in the same way, in billions of litres = ___' does not read as an instruction. The student must infer unaided that they should re-run the whole read-percentage -> decimal -> multiply-by-500 chain using agriculture's 70% share.
fix: Reword to 'Check: repeat the same calculation for agriculture (70% of 500 billion litres), in billions of litres ='

step: Check: the tertiary sector in the same way, in people =  [box expects: 15600]
why: Same condensed-check pattern: no verb, and the student must both find tertiary's percentage on the chart (never given in the walk) and redo the decimal-and-multiply-by-24,000 method entirely unaided.
fix: Reword to 'Check: read tertiary's percentage from the chart and repeat the calculation, in people ='

step: Check: the angle for vans in the same way, in degrees =  [box expects: 60]
why: Vans' count (120) is given in the question, but the instruction never says to use it — 'the angle for vans in the same way' assumes the student remembers to multiply 120 by the 0.5 degrees-per-vehicle figure from two steps earlier without being told to.
fix: Reword to 'Check: multiply the 120 vans by your degrees-per-vehicle figure ='

step: Check: the renewables angle to the nearest degree =  [box expects: 22]
why: Renewables' percentage is never stated anywhere in the walk (only nuclear's 10% was given), so this compressed line silently requires the student to go back to the chart for a new figure AND redo the decimal/x360 method with no breakdown, unlike the scaffolded nuclear steps above it.
fix: Reword to 'Check: read renewables' percentage from the chart, convert to a decimal and multiply by 360 ='

step: Check: abrasion events worked the same way =  [box expects: 80]
why: Abrasion's percentage (40%) is never given in the walk — the student must independently read it off the chart and redo the decimal-times-200 method, but 'worked the same way' is a passive fragment that doesn't say what to do.
fix: Reword to 'Check: read abrasion's percentage from the chart and multiply by the 200 events ='

step: Check: the 10-20 class worked the same way =  [box expects: 30]
why: The 10-20 class's frequency density is never given in text — the student must read a new value off the histogram and multiply it by the class width themselves, but 'worked the same way' doesn't say to do either of those things.
fix: Reword to 'Check: read the 10-20 class's density from the chart and multiply by its width ='

step: Check: the fossil fuels angle to the nearest degree =  [box expects: 227]
why: Fossil fuels' 63% is given in the question, so the data is available, but the line jumps straight to 'the angle' with no verb — it silently expects the student to redo the entire decimal/x360 chain unaided, right after that chain was broken into 3 separate steps for renewables.
fix: Reword to 'Check: convert 63% to a decimal and multiply by 360 for fossil fuels ='

step: Check: migrants from the EU and Other combined =  [box expects: 4400]
why: EU (45%) and Other (10%) are both given in the question, but the phrase names only the answer, not the method — the student must independently remember to add the two percentages, convert to a decimal, and multiply by 8,000, exactly as was scaffolded in 3 separate steps for Asia+Africa above.
fix: Reword to 'Check: add 45% and 10%, convert to a decimal, and multiply by 8,000 ='

step: That share as a decimal:  [box expects: 0.2]
why: Unlike bronze[1] in the same lesson, which spells out '(percentage divided by a hundred)', this step jumps straight to '20% -> 0.2' with no reminder of the method — exactly the kind of unexplained percent-to-decimal jump that trips a weaker reader.
fix: Add the same parenthetical used in bronze[1]: 'That share as a decimal (percentage divided by a hundred):'

step: That share as a decimal:  [box expects: 0.2]
why: Same unexplained percent-to-decimal step as bronze[6]; by silver tier the method has likely been seen once already, so the risk is lower, but the walk still never restates it.
fix: Add '(percentage divided by a hundred)' for consistency with bronze[1].

step: That share as a decimal:  [box expects: 0.1]
why: Repeats the unexplained percent-to-decimal jump seen elsewhere in this lesson.
fix: Add '(percentage divided by a hundred)' as in bronze[1].

step: That share as a decimal:  [box expects: 0.35]
why: Same recurring gap — 35% to 0.35 is never explained in this problem.
fix: Add '(percentage divided by a hundred)' as in bronze[1].

step: That combined share as a decimal:  [box expects: 0.45]
why: Same recurring gap at gold tier — 45% to 0.45 is never explained anywhere in the lesson text itself.
fix: Add '(percentage divided by a hundred)' as in bronze[1].

step: The 20-30 class: density multiplied by its width of 10 gives a frequency of  [box expects: 25]  /  The 30-50 class is 20 wide. Its frequency is  [box expects: 30]
why: The final answer box is in 'people', but neither of these two frequency-density conversion steps is labelled, and 'frequency' is an unfamiliar term dressed up as a plain number here — a student could plausibly leave it as a bare density-derived figure without realising it now represents a headcount.
fix: Label both boxes 'people' (e.g. 'gives a frequency of ___ people').

step: Frequency of the 0-5mm class (density times its width):  [box expects: 20]  /  Frequency of the 5-20mm class:  [box expects: 30]
why: Same frequency-density issue as gold[1]: the final answer is in 'pebbles' but these two conversion steps carry no unit, leaving the meaning of the raw number ambiguous mid-walk.
fix: Label both boxes 'pebbles' (e.g. 'Frequency of the 0-5mm class... = ___ pebbles').

step: the nearest point to the left is at a birth rate of 22, with infant mortality of  [box expects: 32]  /  the nearest point to the right is at a birth rate of 28, with infant mortality of  [box expects: 45]
why: The question and every walk step give raw numbers like '32' and '45' for infant mortality with no unit anywhere in the visible text (only the main answer box metadata says 'per 1000') — a student reading just the walk could reasonably read these as percentages or raw counts rather than a rate per 1,000 births.
fix: Add '(per 1000 births)' to at least the first reading, e.g. 'with infant mortality of ___ per 1000 births'.

step: Check the spacing. Your estimate minus the 35 mm reading gives  [box expects: 2]
why: 'The 35 mm reading' is shorthand for 'the discharge value at 35mm (16 cumecs)', but a struggling reader could easily substitute the literal '35' into the subtraction (18 - 35) instead of the discharge value 16, since the phrase names the axis position, not the quantity being subtracted.
fix: Reword to 'Your estimate minus the discharge at 35 mm (16 cumecs) gives ___ cumecs' and label the box 'cumecs'.

step: intro: A tight rising pattern plus one point far above it: an economy built on oil and gas with very few people to divide the emissions between produces exactly this outlier.
why: This is one long run-on sentence with an embedded colon and the main verb ('produces') held back until the very end — a 15-year-old would likely need to re-read it to work out what is doing the 'producing'.
fix: Split it: 'This is a tight rising pattern with one point far above it. That point is an economy built on oil and gas, with very few people to divide its emissions between — exactly the profile of this kind of outlier.'

step: On the side axis, one gridline step is worth  [box expects: 10]
why: The chart is in mm (established in the question) but this step's wording never repeats the unit, unlike the very next step which reads '...It reads 60 mm.' — a small inconsistency in an otherwise clear problem.
fix: Label the box 'mm'.

step: On the side axis, one labelled step is worth  [box expects: 5]
why: Same gap as bronze[0]: the chart is in °C but this scale-reading step doesn't say so.
fix: Label the box '°C'.

step: One labelled step on the side axis is worth  [box expects: 5000]
why: Population chart's gridline value is given with no unit; less risky than a true scale-conversion trap since the axis is already in raw people-counts, but still an unlabelled number sitting on its own.
fix: Label the box 'people'.

step: The whole 2020 bar reaches the  [box expects: 100 (unit label: ' level')]  /  Together they reach the  [box expects: 24 (unit label: ' level')]
why: 'Reaches the 100 level' and 'reach the 24 level' are unusual phrasings for a percentage stacked bar — GCSE students are used to '100%' and '24%', not '100 level'.
fix: Reword both to use % directly, e.g. 'The whole 2020 bar reaches ___%' and 'Together they reach ___%'.

step: The death rate goes from 25 in 1960 to 12 in 1980, a fall of  [box expects: 13]  (and the birth-rate steps that follow)
why: Birth and death rates are conventionally 'per 1000 population', but this problem never states a unit anywhere — neither in the question nor any walk step — for any of the raw numbers (25, 12, 45, 40, 24, 16). It doesn't block the multiple-choice answer, but leaves every figure in the walk unitless.
fix: Add '(per 1000 population)' to the question stem or the first birth/death rate reading.

step: 450 − 160 =  [box expects: 290 (unit label: ' thousand pounds of change')]
why: The label 'thousand pounds of change' is wordier and less natural than the '£ ___ thousand' format used everywhere else in the same problem, and 'of change' is redundant once the subtraction is shown.
fix: Shorten the label to 'thousand pounds' (or '£ thousand') to match the earlier steps.

step: Over the same stretch visitors go from 200 to 800, a rise of  [box expects: 600]
why: The paired step just above it ('a rise of 6 hours') is unit-labelled, but this visitor-count step isn't, which reads as an inconsistency even though 'visitors' is contextually obvious.
fix: Label the box 'visitors' to match the parallel 'hours' label above it.

step: The point furthest right, at 99% literacy, has a birth rate of  [box expects: 9]  (and 'At 70% literacy the birth rate is  [box expects: 25]')
why: The very first reading in this problem says 'Its birth rate per 1000 is 42', establishing the unit, but the next two birth-rate readings drop 'per 1000' entirely — a minor inconsistency that could leave a student unsure whether later numbers are the same measure.
fix: Repeat 'per 1000' in the later steps too, e.g. 'has a birth rate per 1000 of ___'.

step: Read the male bar for 0-4 off the scale.  [box expects: 7.1]
why: Nothing in this question (country-type-from-shape, MC) ever says the pyramid bars are percentages. The box has no unit and the final answer is a lettered MC choice with no unit either, so a student typing '7.1' has zero textual confirmation this is a percent-of-population reading rather than millions/thousands. Same problem repeats on the next three steps in this walk (0.8, 6.3, 13.8).
fix: Show '%' to the right of the box on every bar-reading/adding step in this walk (7.1, 0.8, 6.3, 13.8), not just on problems whose final answer happens to be a percentage.

step: How much longer is the 0-4 male bar than the 60-64 male bar?  [box expects: 6.3]
why: 'Longer' frames this as a bar-length/physical-distance question, when the value being subtracted is actually a percentage-point difference. A student could reasonably think they need to measure the bars in cm.
fix: Reword to "How much bigger is the 0-4 percentage than the 60-64 percentage?" and label the box '%'.

step: Read the male bar for 0-4.  [box expects: 7.1] / Add them to get the whole 0-4 band. [box expects: 13.8]
why: The question stem does say 'highest percentage of the population', so there's some context, but none of the four bar-reading/summing boxes in the walk itself repeat '%' — a student could still start entering raw-looking numbers without the percent frame in front of them at the moment of typing.
fix: Add '%' to the box on every bar-read/sum step (7.1, 6.7, 13.8, 6.8).

step: Now do the same for 30-34 to compare.  [box expects: 6.8]
why: "Do the same" is a vague back-reference to a two-part process two steps back (read male bar, read female bar, add them) but only one number is asked for here. A student may read the male bar for 30-34 only and stop, not realising two bars need adding.
fix: Spell it out: "Now read the male and female bars for 30-34 and add them together."

step: Warm up on the row above it: read the male bar for 45-49. [box expects: 3.8] / Now read the male bar for 40-44. [box expects: 3.7]
why: The question stem and main answer box already establish '%' for this problem, so context is strong, but the intermediate boxes still show no unit, breaking consistency with the final box.
fix: Show '%' on the intermediate boxes too, purely for consistency.

step: Add the two dependant groups together.  [box expects: 48]
why: "The two dependant groups" is a back-reference to the 44% (given in the question) and the 4% (given two steps earlier) — neither number is restated here, so a student has to hold both in memory across steps.
fix: "Add the under-15 group (44%) and the over-65 group (4%) together."

step: Divide dependants by workers and multiply by 100. Give a whole number.  [box expects: 92]
why: The previous three steps in this same walk were all percentages (44, 56, 48), so a student is primed to also append a '%' to this answer — but a dependency ratio is not a percentage, even though it's calculated the same way. There is no label to break that habit. "Give a whole number" is also vaguer than the "to the nearest whole number" phrasing used elsewhere in this lesson (e.g. gold[0], gold[3]), leaving rounding-vs-truncating unclear.
fix: Label the box '(a ratio — no % sign)' and reword to "...multiply by 100, rounded to the nearest whole number."

step: Check: take your ratio away from 100.  [box expects: 8]
why: The step never explains what this arithmetic is actually checking, so a student can do the subtraction correctly without understanding why, or wonder if they've misread the task.
fix: Add a one-clause reason, e.g. "As a rough sanity check, see how far below 100 your ratio sits."

step: Counting the top bar as row 1 and working down, which row number is 65-69?  [box expects: 3]
why: Every other pyramid problem in this lesson counts 'the bottom bar as row 1'. This problem silently flips the direction. A student who has just done several bottom-up problems is likely to apply the same habit here without noticing the switch.
fix: Make the change explicit: "Unlike earlier questions, count from the TOP this time — the top bar is row 1."

step: Add the three male bars for 65-69, 70-74 and 75+.  [box expects: 8.5]
why: Main answer box already shows '%' so context is decent, but this and the next summing step (10.6) are unlabeled.
fix: Add '%' to both intermediate sum boxes for consistency.

step: Read the male bar for 0-4.  [box expects: 2] / Read the male bar for that widest row, 45-49. [box expects: 4.4]
why: This question (Germany narrow base -> population decline, MC) never mentions percentages anywhere, and the MC final answer has no unit either. A student has no textual cue that 2 and 4.4 are percent-of-population readings.
fix: Show '%' on both bar-reading boxes (and on the base-check sum, 3.8).

step: How many times wider is the widest male bar than the 0-4 male bar?  [box expects: 2.2]
why: This answer is a unitless multiplier (a ratio of two percentages), but coming right after two unlabeled percentage-reading steps, a student could easily assume it's also a percentage and second-guess a correct '2.2'.
fix: Label the box '(a multiplier, e.g. 2.2 — not a %)'.

step: How many rows are there from 15-19 up to 60-64 inclusive?  [box expects: 10]
why: The walk only ever establishes the row number for 15-19 (row 4). It never asks for, or states, the row number for 60-64 (row 13). To answer '10' the student must silently work out the second endpoint's row themselves and then do inclusive counting — a skill never demonstrated earlier in the walk.
fix: Insert a step first: "Which row number is 60-64?" so both endpoints are on the table before asking for the inclusive count.

step: Add the male bars for those ten rows.  [box expects: 30.0] / Now add the female bars for the same ten rows. [box expects: 26.2]
why: Main box shows '%', giving decent context, but these two summing boxes are unlabeled.
fix: Add '%' to both boxes.

step: Now divide dependants by workers and multiply by 100, to the nearest whole number.  [box expects: 85]
why: Same ratio-vs-percentage confusion as bronze[6]: the two steps immediately before this were percentages (46%, 54%), so the habit of expecting a % carries over even though the correct main-box unit here is '(none)'.
fix: Label the box '(a ratio, not a %)'.

step: The narrowing base holds children born in the last five years, so from which year onwards?  [box expects: 2020]
why: Getting 2020 requires remembering '2025' as the survey year, which was stated three steps earlier in the walk's intro and never restated here.
fix: "Using 2025 as the survey year again, the narrowing base holds children born in the last five years — so from which year onwards?"

step: Divide dependants by workers and multiply by 100, to the nearest whole number.  [box expects: 89]
why: Same recurring ratio-vs-% issue: preceding steps (47%, 53%) are percentages, this one is not, and the box carries no label to signal the change.
fix: Label the box '(a ratio, not a %)'.

step: Check: take your new ratio away from 100.  [box expects: 11]
why: As with bronze[6], the purpose of subtracting from 100 is never explained, so the check step teaches nothing to a student who does it correctly.
fix: Add a short reason for the check, or drop it if it isn't pedagogically necessary.

step: And someone aged 65 today?  [box expects: 85]
why: Sentence fragment leaning entirely on the previous full sentence's template ('...will be how old in 20 years?'). Usually inferable, but strictly incomplete.
fix: "And how old will someone aged 65 today be in 20 years?"

step: And someone aged 35?  [box expects: 1990]
why: Same ellipsis pattern as bronze[5] — relies on the prior sentence's structure ('...was born in which year?').
fix: "And someone aged 35 — which year were they born?"

step: And someone aged 30?  [box expects: 1995]
why: Same recurring ellipsis pattern.
fix: "And someone aged 30 — which year were they born?"

step: And someone aged 80?  [box expects: 1935]
why: Same recurring ellipsis pattern.
fix: "And someone aged 80 — which year were they born?"

step: Parkland and industrial each appear how many times?  [box expects: 1]
why: The plural framing ('Parkland and industrial each appear...') reads like it wants two separate counts, when actually only one shared number is expected because both happen to tie.
fix: "Parkland and industrial both appear the same number of times — how many is that?"

step: Q1 is the middle of the lower four, so average the 2nd and 3rd sorted values. What is Q1 in m/s?  [box expects: 0.85]
why: The eight velocities are given unsorted in the question (0.8, 1.2, 0.9, 1.5, 1.1, 1.3, 0.7, 1.0). The walk never displays the sorted order, so the student must correctly sort all eight in their head before they can even find 'the 2nd and 3rd sorted values'. A sorting slip breaks everything downstream.
fix: Show the sorted list explicitly: "Sorted: 0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.5."

step: Which beach has the smaller range? Type 1 for Beach A or 2 for Beach B.  [box expects: 2]
why: Every other box in this lesson expects a real measurement value. This step suddenly switches to an arbitrary numeric code (1/2) for a letter choice, which is a different convention a student hasn't been primed for — they may type 'A'/'B' or the range value instead of '2'.
fix: Accept the letter directly: "Type A or B."

step: Q1 is the middle of the lower six, so average the 3rd and 4th sorted values. What is Q1, in metres?  [box expects: 2.85]
why: Twelve unsorted river-width values (2.1, 3.4, 2.8, 5.2, 3.1, 2.5, 4.8, 3.6, 2.9, 3.3, 4.1, 3.0) must be mentally sorted with zero scaffolding shown — harder than the 8-value silver version of the same problem type, and a single misordering invalidates Q1, Q3 and the IQR.
fix: Display the sorted list before asking for Q1: "Sorted: 2.1, 2.5, 2.8, 2.9, 3.0, 3.1, 3.3, 3.4, 3.6, 4.1, 4.8, 5.2."

step: Sorted, the middle pair sit in positions 5 and 6. Average them to get the median, in ppm.  [box expects: 402.5]
why: Ten unsorted CO2 readings (including the extreme outlier 1200) must be sorted mentally before the student can find positions 5 and 6 — the sorted list is never shown, unlike some other problems in this lesson (e.g. silver[6]) that do show it.

step: Subtract Q1 from Q3 to get the IQR, then check it comes out below the full range of 23.  [box expects: 13]
why: The sentence bundles two instructions (compute the IQR; verify a check against the range) but there is only one answer box. A student may be unsure whether the check itself needs a typed response, or may try to type something related to '23'.
fix: End the question at "Subtract Q1 from Q3 to get the IQR." and present the range comparison as separate feedback text after the answer is submitted, not as part of the instruction.

step: Subtract Q1 from Q3 to get the IQR, then check it comes out below the full range of 14.  [box expects: 8]
why: Same compound-instruction pattern as bronze[7] — one box, two asks.
fix: Split the check out of the question text, as above.

step: Subtract Q1 from Q3 to get the IQR, then check it comes out below the full range of 3.2.  [box expects: 1.7]
why: Same compound-instruction pattern recurring a third time in this lesson.
fix: Split the check out of the question text, as above.

step: Add the two middle values of that upper half, the 3rd and 4th of the six.  [box expects: 31]
why: The question explicitly instructs 'First put in order, then find Q3', flagging that the raw data (given in calendar order, with two repeated values — 6 and 8 each appear twice) needs reordering. But the walk only ever confirms the smallest value (5); the full sorted list is never shown. The student must correctly reorder all twelve values, including the duplicates, entirely unaided before they can isolate 'the 3rd and 4th of the six' in the upper half.
fix: Show the full sorted list: "Sorted: 5, 6, 6, 8, 8, 10, 12, 13, 15, 16, 17, 18."

step: Find the row labelled Urban. Reading down to the scale, what value does the left edge of its shaded box sit on?  [box expects: 18]
why: The value read is a temperature (matching the main box's °C), but this box-plot-reading step doesn't restate the unit the way the equivalent gold[0] problem does ('in metres').
fix: Add '°C' to this step and the next one (right edge, 31), matching the phrasing used in gold[0].

step: QUESTION: ...An outlier is defined as more than 1.5 × IQR above Q3. Is 15.8 an outlier? Enter Q3 + 1.5 × IQR (the outlier boundary).
why: The question leads with a yes/no-shaped question ('Is 15.8 an outlier?') but the actual required answer is a specific number — the boundary value, 24.25 — not a yes/no judgement and not 15.8 itself. A student reading top-to-bottom is very likely to try answering the rhetorical question literally.
fix: Remove or clearly subordinate the framing question, e.g.: "An outlier is more than 1.5×IQR above Q3. Calculate the outlier boundary (Q3 + 1.5×IQR) so you can check whether 15.8 counts as one."

step: Add that to Q3 to get the boundary, then compare it with the largest value of 15.8.  [box expects: 24.25]
why: Same compound-instruction issue as the bronze[7]/silver[6]/gold[2] pattern, and it compounds the question-level ambiguity above (finding for the gold[3] question stem) about whether a comparison verdict is also expected.
fix: End the instruction at "...to get the boundary." and drop the comparison clause from the graded step.

step: The lower half is the five values below the median. Give its middle value. This is Q1.  [box expects: -8]
why: This is the first negative answer in either lesson pack, introduced with no warning that a negative value is expected. The eleven mixed-sign migration values are also never shown in sorted order, so the student must both sort numbers with mixed signs and correctly type a negative result, unaided, for the first time here.
fix: Show the sorted list and flag the sign explicitly: "Sorted: -45, -20, -8, 5, 12, 25, 38, 52, 71, 95, 120 — note some values are negative."

step: Now compare that rise with the value you started from. 500 ÷ 2000 =
why: Box has no unit and every other box around it in this same problem is about percentages (the very next box, 0.25 × 100, IS labelled %). A student mid-percentage-question with no cue may type 25 here instead of 0.25.
fix: Label the box '(a decimal)' so it visually contrasts with the % box that follows.

step: Now compare that fall with the value you started from. 18 ÷ 120 =
why: Same pattern: unlabelled decimal step immediately before a %-labelled step, in a question that is entirely about percentages.
fix: Label the box '(a decimal)'.

step: Now compare that rise with the value you started from. 10 ÷ 50 =
why: Same recurring pattern — unlabelled ratio step directly before the %-labelled step.
fix: Label the box '(a decimal)'.

step: Now divide the part by the whole, in that order. 240 ÷ 800 =
why: No unit shown for a bare-decimal answer, sitting next to a %-labelled box one line later — same trap as the others.
fix: Label the box '(a decimal)'.

step: Now compare that fall with the value you started from. 0.5 ÷ 5 =
why: Unlabelled decimal box immediately before a %-labelled box in a percentage-decrease question.
fix: Label the box '(a decimal)'.

step: Now compare that rise with the value you started from. 60000 ÷ 150000 =
why: Same unlabelled-decimal-before-%-box pattern.
fix: Label the box '(a decimal)'.

step: Divide the part by the whole, in that order. 175 ÷ 500 =
why: Same pattern — no unit on the ratio step, % unit on the very next step.
fix: Label the box '(a decimal)'.

step: Now compare that fall with the value you started from. 5 ÷ 40 =
why: Same recurring trap.
fix: Label the box '(a decimal)'.

step: Now compare that fall with the value you started from. 3720 ÷ 12400 =
why: Same recurring trap, larger numbers make the decimal/percent confusion even easier to fall into.
fix: Label the box '(a decimal)'.

step: Now compare that rise with the value you started from. 1.5 ÷ 2 =
why: Same recurring trap.
fix: Label the box '(a decimal)'.

step: Now the proportion: part ÷ whole. 25 ÷ 100 =
why: Same recurring trap — note the box immediately before it (total = 100) IS labelled 'ha', making the unlabelled decimal box stand out as inconsistent.
fix: Label the box '(a decimal)'.

step: Now compare that rise with the value you started from. 2730 ÷ 4200 =
why: Same recurring trap.
fix: Label the box '(a decimal)'.

step: Now compare that rise with the value you started from. 0.63 ÷ 1.8 =
why: Same recurring trap.
fix: Label the box '(a decimal)'.

step: Now compare that fall with the value you started from. 99 ÷ 450 =
why: Same recurring trap.
fix: Label the box '(a decimal)'.

step: Now compare that fall with the value you started from. 63 ÷ 420 =
why: Same recurring trap.
fix: Label the box '(a decimal)'.

why: Same decimal-vs-percent ambiguity as the bronze/silver ratio steps, just appearing in a check line late in the walk rather than the main path.
fix: Label the box '(a decimal)'.

step: Rough check: 5 ÷ 25 × 100 =
why: This is a ×100 computation in the same form as the graded answer two steps above (5 ÷ 24 × 100, to 1 decimal place = 20.8, which IS labelled %), but this box carries no % label — the inconsistency could make a student unsure whether to write 20 or 0.2.
fix: Label the box '%' to match the parallel graded step.

step: Now the Primary bar in the 2020 group:
why: This is a sentence fragment (no verb, just a trailing colon) and it drops the 'in % of the workforce' unit that the fully-worded step immediately above it supplied. A student has to guess both what's being asked for and what unit to answer in.
fix: "Now read the Primary bar in the 2020 group. Its height, in % of the workforce, is"

step: Nigeria's projected 2050 bar reads
why: The parallel step directly above it states the unit ('Nigeria's 2020 bar, in millions, reads'); this one drops 'in millions'. The unit is inferable from the previous line, but the inconsistency is unnecessary and a careful reader may pause on it.
fix: "Nigeria's projected 2050 bar, in millions, reads"

step: P lies south of the 8°C line, so P is warmer than 8. Type the lowest whole temperature P could be, in °C.
why: The sentence states P is strictly warmer than 8, then asks for 'the lowest whole temperature P could be' and expects the answer to be 8 itself. Read literally, the lowest whole number strictly greater than 8 is 9 — a careful student following the stated inequality is likely to answer 9 and be marked wrong.
fix: Reword to avoid the contradiction, e.g. "P is warmer than 8°C, so treat 8°C as your boundary estimate for P. Type that boundary value, in °C."

step: Type the largest total, in £, those 80 lower-earning households could contribute.
why: Every other step in this walk states the operation to perform (divide, multiply, subtract). This step jumps straight to a result (2,000,000) without ever telling the student to multiply 80 by the £25,000 ceiling — they aren't told how to get the number, only what the number represents.
fix: "80 households × the most any one of them could earn (£25,000) ="

step: Type the smallest total, in £, the remaining 20 households must contribute.
why: Same gap as the step above — it never says to subtract the previous total from the area's implied total income (£4,500,000) to get this figure.
fix: "Subtract that from the area's total income (£4,500,000) to get what the remaining 20 households must contribute:"

step: If no red arrowhead lands on London, how many red arrows must instead begin at London?
why: This presumes every red arrow on the map connects to London (starts or ends there) — a fact never stated anywhere in the walk. A careful student could reasonably object that the red arrows might run between two other cities entirely.
fix: Add a line establishing the map's scope before this step, e.g. "All the arrows drawn on this map run to or from London."

step: The Leeds arrow is half as wide. Flow widths scale straight, so halve that value.
why: 'Scale straight' is not standard phrasing for a 15-year-old and doesn't clearly mean 'directly proportional' on first read.
fix: "Flow widths are directly proportional to the number of people, so halve that value."

step: Type the position of the economic option, counting 1 down to 4.
why: Every other 'counting 1 ... down to 4 ...' instruction in this pack names what options 1 and 4 actually are (e.g. 'counting 1 for towards London down to 4 for commuter journeys'). This one just says '1 down to 4' with no anchor, breaking the pattern the student has been trained to rely on.
fix: "counting 1 for weather down to 4 for universities"

step: How many times bigger does the drawing look than the data really is? Divide the area factor by the data factor, to the nearest whole number.
why: 'The area factor' and 'the data factor' are never introduced under those names in the two steps that actually computed them (100 and 29) — the student has to guess which earlier number each label refers back to.
fix: Name the values when they're first computed, e.g. "...how many times the area does it have? (this is the area factor)" and "...divide London's population by Newcastle's (this is the data factor)", then this step can safely refer back to them by name.

step: How many of the three ranges are bigger than 1.0 m?
why: The question stem never states units for the river-width readings (3.2, 3.4, 3.3...); this step suddenly introduces 'm' as an established unit that a careful student never saw defined.
fix: Add units to the question stem, e.g. 'gets (in metres): Site 1: 3.2, 3.4, 3.3...', or drop 'm' from this step and just say 'bigger than 1.0'.

step: Do not argue this one, test it.
why: Blunt, idiomatic phrasing is an unusual register for an instruction and could make a struggling reader pause to parse it rather than telling them what to do next.
fix: Reword to something plainer, e.g. 'You don't need to argue this in words — test it with numbers instead.'

step: Every number it gives you has to be screened against the numbering first.
why: 'Screened against the numbering' is abstract phrasing for what is actually a simple check (is the number bigger than the highest square number?); a 15-year-old may need to re-read it.
fix: Reword to 'Every number has to be checked against the highest square number first.'

step: (no WALK section provided at all)
why: Unlike every other problem in this pack, gold[4] has no step-by-step walk — just the question and four options with zero scaffolding. May be intentional (an unscaffolded reasoning check) but is worth confirming it wasn't dropped by the pipeline.
fix: Confirm whether a walk was intended; if so, add one ending in an explicit 'choose that option' resolution like the other gold-tier MC questions.

step: Divide that reading by 0.5, a typical value here, to see how far out it is.
why: 'A typical value here' is vague about where 0.5 comes from — it's a rounded midpoint of the six normal readings (0.3–0.6), not a value literally in the list — and a careful student may wonder why 0.5 specifically.
fix: Reword to 'Divide by 0.5, roughly the middle of the six normal readings, to see how many times bigger the anomaly is.'

step: Join the two pairs, easting first, into one four figure reference and type it.
why: By this step the student has read the vertical-line number (step 1) and horizontal-line number (step 2), but neither step ever labelled which was the 'easting' and which the 'northing' — the walk assumes the student already knows vertical=easting, horizontal=northing, a convention never explicitly named until this final step.
fix: Add the label at the point each is read, e.g. step 1: 'This vertical line is the easting — read its number...'; step 2: 'This horizontal line is the northing — read its number...'

step: Join the two pairs, easting first, into one four figure reference and type it.
why: The box wants a bare 4-digit string (8332) with no space, but the instruction only says 'join the two pairs' — having just typed '83' and '32' as separate answers, a student may reasonably write '83 32' when told to join them.
fix: State explicitly: 'Join them with no space between, easting first, to make one four-figure number (e.g. 8332), and type it.' Box label should read '(4-figure ref, no space)'.

step: Join the two pairs, easting first, into one four figure reference and type it.
why: Same issue as bronze[0]: no instruction that the four digits must be typed together with no space (expects 8532).
fix: State explicitly: 'Join them with no space between, easting first (e.g. 8532).' Box label should read '(4-figure ref, no space)'.

step: Join the two pairs, easting first, into one four-figure reference and type it.
why: Same issue: no instruction that the four digits must be typed together with no space (expects 6841).
fix: State explicitly: 'Join them with no space between, easting first (e.g. 6841).' Box label should read '(4-figure ref, no space)'.

step: Join the two pairs, easting first, into one four-figure reference and type it.

step: Join the two pairs, easting first, into one four figure reference and type it.
why: Same issue: no instruction that the four digits must be typed together with no space (expects 4018).
fix: State explicitly: 'Join them with no space between, easting first (e.g. 4018).' Box label should read '(4-figure ref, no space)'.

step: Put the three easting figures first, then the three northing figures, and type the six figure reference.
why: The box wants a bare 6-digit string (842324) with no space, but the instruction never says so; having just typed the easting block and northing block as separate answers, a student may write them with a space (e.g. '842 324').
fix: State explicitly: 'Type all six figures together with no space, easting first (e.g. 842324).' Box label should read '(6-figure ref, no space)'.

step: Put the three easting figures first, then the three northing figures, and type the six figure reference.
why: Same issue: no 'no space' instruction on the final join (expects 686413).
fix: State explicitly: 'Type all six figures together with no space, easting first (e.g. 686413).' Box label should read '(6-figure ref, no space)'.

step: Put the three easting figures first, then the three northing figures, and type the six-figure reference.
why: The two half-blocks were each built with the clear instruction 'type all three figures together', but the final combining step drops that language and expects 677422 with no space — the clarity doesn't carry through to the step that matters most.
fix: Reuse the same wording: 'Now type all six figures together with no space, easting first (e.g. 677422).'

step: It sits almost level with it rather than clearly above or below. Type 1 for a straight compass point, or 2 for a diagonal.
why: The walk ends here — it never states the resulting compass direction (East) or which of the 8 multiple-choice options to pick, unlike sibling problems (bronze[3]/[4]/[6]) which close with an explicit 'the answer is X' line. A student can complete every step correctly and still not know which option to select.
fix: Add a final resolving line, e.g. 'Right + level = due East. Choose the E option.'

step: It sits almost straight above, barely off to either side. Type 1 for due north, or 2 for north-east.
why: As in bronze[1], the walk stops after this step without ever stating the resulting compass direction or which multiple-choice option it matches — no closing 'the answer is N' line like the 8-way-code problems get.
fix: Add a final line, e.g. 'Almost directly above = due North. Choose the N option.'

step: It sits almost straight above, barely off to either side. Type 1 for due north, or 2 for north-east.
why: 'Almost straight above, barely off to either side' is self-contradictory to a careful reader — saying a feature is 'barely off to either side' suggests a slight lean towards NE or NW, which could make a student doubt the intended answer of due north.
fix: Reword to something less hedged, e.g. 'It sits almost directly above, not leaning clearly to the east or west, so this is a straight compass point rather than a diagonal.'

step: It sits almost level with it rather than clearly above or below. Type 1 for a straight compass point, or 2 for a diagonal.
why: Same pattern as bronze[1]/silver[4]: the walk ends without ever stating the resulting compass letter or which multiple-choice option to pick.
fix: Add a final resolving line, e.g. 'Right and level = due East. Choose that option.'

step: Check by turning round: from the upland, Castleton lies in the exact opposite direction. Type its number from the same list.
why: 'The same list' vaguely refers back to the N=1…NW=8 code list given two steps earlier without restating it; a struggling student has to scroll back up and hold all 8 codes in mind to answer this check.
fix: Restate the code list inline, e.g. 'Using N=1, NE=2, E=3, SE=4, S=5, SW=6, W=7, NW=8 again, type the number for the opposite direction.'

step: Check by turning round: from Hare Runs, the roundabout lies in the exact opposite direction. Type its number from the same list.
why: Same vague back-reference to 'the same list' as bronze[3], two steps after the code list was given.
fix: Restate the code list inline, e.g. 'Using N=1, NE=2, E=3, SE=4, S=5, SW=6, W=7, NW=8 again, type the number for the opposite direction.'

step: Check by turning round: from Pendle Hill, Worston lies in the exact opposite direction. Type its number from the same list.
why: Same vague back-reference to 'the same list' as bronze[3]/[4].
fix: Restate the code list inline, e.g. 'Using N=1, NE=2, E=3, SE=4, S=5, SW=6, W=7, NW=8 again, type the number for the opposite direction.'

step: Check by turning round: from Castleton, Riding House Farm lies in the exact opposite direction. Type its number from the same list.
why: Same vague back-reference to 'the same list' as the bronze compass problems.
fix: Restate the code list inline, e.g. 'Using N=1, NE=2, E=3, SE=4, S=5, SW=6, W=7, NW=8 again, type the number for the opposite direction.'

step: Check by turning round: from Only Grange Farm, Castleton lies in the exact opposite direction. Type its number from the same list.
why: Same vague back-reference to 'the same list'. Note gold[0], a sibling gold problem, avoids this by restating 'Using N=1, NE=2, E=3, SE=4' directly — a better model to follow.
fix: Restate the code list inline, e.g. 'Using N=1, NE=2, E=3, SE=4, S=5, SW=6, W=7, NW=8 again, type the number for the opposite direction.'

step: Measure between them and give the distance in km, to the nearest 0.5 km.
why: This step explicitly says 'to the nearest 0.5 km' and expects the padded decimal '2.0' — but the equivalent instruction in gold[4] ('The question asks for the nearest 0.5 km. Type the distance in km.') expects a bare '2' for the same kind of whole-km value. The wording never tells the student whether a whole-km answer needs a trailing '.0'.
fix: Pick one convention and state it next to the box, e.g. '(always show 1 decimal place, e.g. 2.0)', and apply it consistently wherever 'nearest 0.5 km' is used.

step: The question asks for the nearest 0.5 km. Type the distance in km.
why: Same inconsistency as bronze[2] in reverse: here a whole-km result (2) is expected bare with no decimal, while bronze[2]'s equivalent step for the same kind of value expects '2.0'. A student can't tell from the wording alone whether trailing zeros matter.
fix: State the decimal-place rule explicitly (e.g. always 1 decimal place) and apply it consistently across all 'nearest 0.5 km' steps.

step: Start on the map. Go along the bottom edge to the line labelled 47, then up the side to the line labelled 63: the first house sits in that square. Type the easting of the line along the right-hand edge of that square.
why: This step asks the student to find and type the easting of the square's right-hand edge line (48), but that value is never used again — the very next steps just re-extract the digits '476' and '488' directly from the numbers already given in the question text. The step introduces a concept and an answer that goes nowhere, which is disorienting for a student trying to track how each answer feeds the next.
fix: Either drop this step, or make its output actually feed into the working, so every step visibly contributes to the final answer.

step: In kilometres the two legs are 1.2 and 1.1. Type 1.2 squared added to 1.1 squared.
why: Mixing prose and numbers ('1.2 squared added to 1.1 squared') is an awkward way to say 1.2² + 1.1²; a struggling reader may need a second pass to parse the order of operations.
fix: Reword as 'Square 1.2, square 1.1, then add the two results together' or show it as 1.2² + 1.1².

step: ask step 3: "Now read the brown number printed on the contour line that circles the hill. Type it." (box expects 200)
why: The step never says this number is a height in metres — it just says "read the brown number... Type it." The main question stem said so, but three steps in a struggling reader may have lost that thread, and this mini-box carries no unit hint at all. The sibling step in silver[4] for the same hill DOES add ", in metres", so this is an inconsistency, not a deliberate omission.
fix: Add the unit cue used elsewhere in the pack: "Now read the brown number printed on the contour line that circles the hill. Type the height, in metres." Box label: "m".

step: ask step 2: "Type the number printed on the thick brown loop that runs round the fell." (box expects 600)
why: This problem's question is about naming a landform, not reading a height, so nothing here tells the student the loop's number is a height in metres — unlike the equivalent steps elsewhere in the pack that add ", in metres".
fix: Reword to: "Type the number printed on the thick brown loop that runs round the fell, in metres." Box label: "m".

step: ask step 1: "Type the northing of the horizontal grid line immediately below the Stone Arthur label." (box expects 9)
why: Every other northing/easting box on this map is a two-figure number (43, 77, 88...). Here the expected answer is the single figure 9, which only makes sense if this map prints its northings with a leading zero (the line is actually labelled "09"). L14 silver[1] explicitly warns about exactly this ("ignoring any leading zero... this map's northings are printed with a leading zero"), but L13 never does — so a student reading "09" off the map has no way to know whether to type 9 or 09.
fix: Add the same caveat used in L14: "Type the northing of that line — this map prints its northings with a leading zero, so 09 is typed as 9." Box label: "(figure only, drop any leading zero)".

step: ask step 4: "Divide the distance along by the height up. Type the answer." (box expects 10)
why: This is the step that produces the n in the "1 in n" gradient ratio, and it's the one place in the whole pack with zero unit or format framing — no "in metres", no "no unit needed", nothing linking the number back to the ratio the question asked for. A struggling student could easily write "1 in 10", or "0.1", or freeze over what kind of number 10 is supposed to represent.
fix: Reword to: "Divide the distance along by the height up. Type the number that completes the ratio — this is the n in '1 in n', so no unit is needed." Box label: "(ratio figure, no unit)".

step: intro: "The same points test works for both landforms, so read the direction before you name anything."
why: "The same points test" refers back to the valley-vs-spur method taught in a different problem (silver[2]) that this problem never restates. A student who reaches silver[3] without just having done silver[2] hits a dangling reference at the very start — though the later steps do re-teach the rule by the end, so it's confusing rather than blocking.
fix: Make the opener self-contained: "Contours bend into points wherever they cross a slope — the direction the point faces tells spurs and valleys apart. Read the direction before you name anything."

step: intro: "Gradient is height gained divided by ground covered. The units you divide in are the units you answer in."
why: The second sentence is compressed and abstract — a struggling reader has to do extra translation work to turn "the units you divide in are the units you answer in" into "metres divided by km gives metres per km".
fix: Rewrite as: "Gradient is height gained divided by ground covered. Divide metres by kilometres and the answer comes out in metres per kilometre."

step: ask step 1: "Find Castleton, the largest settlement on the extract, near the middle where the main road widens into streets. Type 1 once you have it."
why: This step doesn't test anything about the map — it just asks the student to type 1 once they think they've found the village, with no real check on whether they found the right place. A struggling student may wonder what's actually being asked, or worry that "1" is a real answer they could get wrong.
fix: Either drop this step, or turn it into a genuine check, e.g. "Type the number of roads that meet at Castleton."

step: ask step 3: "Now read the number printed in the break in the thick ring, just above and right of the hill's name. Type it." (box expects 200)
why: Same pattern as L13 bronze[0]: this is the "read the raw number" step and it drops the ", in metres" qualifier used on equivalent steps elsewhere in this pack, even though the main question already calls the number a height.
fix: Reword to: "...Type the height, in metres." Box label: "m".

step: ask step 4: "Check the alternative. Type the number of sides of that road that carry houses: 1 if they all sit on one side, 2 if they line both sides."
why: The sentence first asks for "the number of sides... that carry houses" as if it wants a count, then immediately redefines the same box as a 1/2 code. Both framings happen to give the same digit here, but the double phrasing makes a student re-read to work out which one they're actually answering.
fix: Use one framing only: "Type 1 if the houses sit on only one side of the road, or 2 if they line both sides."

step: ask step 4: "Now compare their heights on the page. Type 1 if the hill is higher up the map than the village, 2 if it is lower down."
why: This Map Interpretation lesson follows straight on from a Contours lesson where "height" always meant elevation in metres. Here "heights on the page" actually means north-south position — a different sense of the same word — and nothing flags the switch, risking a struggler reading "higher" as "higher elevation".
fix: Avoid the word height for page position: "Now compare how far up the page each one sits. Type 1 if the hill sits further north (higher up the page) than the village, or 2 if it sits further south."

step: ask step 5: "Check by turning round. Using N=1, NE=2, E=3, SE=4, S=5, SW=6, W=7, NW=8, type the number for the direction of the village from the hill."
why: Eight compass codes are packed into one sentence, and the student also has to reverse the direction they just worked out (village-from-hill instead of hill-from-village). It's fully spelled out so it's answerable, but it's a lot to hold in working memory at once for a struggling reader.
fix: Split across two sentences: state the code list first, then the question — e.g. "N=1, NE=2, E=3, SE=4, S=5, SW=6, W=7, NW=8. Now type the code for the direction of the village from the hill (the reverse of the direction you just found)."

step: ask step 4: "Now compare the rows. Type 1 if the two are almost level on the page, 2 if one is far higher up than the other."
why: Same "higher up" page-position phrasing as silver[0] step 4. The word "rows" gives more context here so it's less likely to be misread as elevation, but it repeats the same risky word choice.
fix: Say "further north" or "further up the page" instead of "higher up" to keep it clearly separate from contour height.

step: option 0: "The west is low, near the contour labelled 100 m, with widely spaced contours and a main road along the valley floor, while the land eastwards climbs steeply past the contour labelled 550 m"
why: A single 40-plus-word sentence stacks four separate facts (height, spacing, road, opposite height) with no break beyond commas. A struggling reader has to hold all four clauses in mind at once to compare it against three much shorter distractor options.
fix: Split into two sentences: "The west is low ground, close to the 100 m contour, with widely spaced contours and a road along the valley floor. The land to the east climbs steeply, past the 550 m contour."

step: option 0: "It keeps to lower, gently sloping ground where the contour lines are widely spaced, rather than climbing the hill ringed by the 200 m contour"
why: A single long sentence combining a positive claim with a contrastive comparison ("rather than...") — readable, but noticeably denser than the other three options.
fix: Split it: "It keeps to lower, gently sloping ground where the contours are widely spaced. It does not climb the hill ringed by the 200 m contour."

step: option 0: "Gently sloping valley-floor land beside a stream, with a main road running the length of the dale and higher ground rising on either side"
why: A single sentence fragment (no main verb) stacking three separate pieces of evidence; a struggling reader may need to re-read it to unpack all three.
fix: Turn it into a full, itemised sentence: "The village sits on gently sloping valley-floor land beside a stream. A main road runs the length of the dale, and higher ground rises on either side."

step: option 0: "Square 9893: woodland shading covers roughly four fifths of it and straight tracks run through the trees, with almost no buildings"
why: Combines a fraction ("four fifths"), a described map feature, and a negative claim in one sentence — more to parse than the single-fact distractors it's competing against.
fix: Split into shorter clauses: "Square 9893: woodland covers most of it. Straight tracks run through the trees, and almost no buildings are drawn."
